atlas-lt.0061: VU Career Days (Vilnius University, 23 to 27 March 2026: fair, quick interviews, a LinkedIn workshop in English and a hackathon) and the Vilnius Tech Career Day (23rd edition, registration for 2027 open).
atlas-lt.0062: No national season; the peaks follow the student year: Swedbank hires trainees most actively from February to May, VU Career Days are in March, and the Luminor programme we read closed its applications on 30 May.
atlas-lt.0063: The programmes we read take a bachelor’s or a master’s (Luminor asked for a BSc or MSc with 0 to 3 years of experience) and Swedbank states no degree level; none asks for a master’s.
atlas-lt.0064: Only regulated professions need recognition: the competent authority decides within three months of receiving all documents and can require an adaptation period of up to three years or an aptitude test; documents are translated into Lithuanian with a certified translation. Where Lithuania does not regulate the profession, you apply directly to the employer. SKVC is the ENIC/NARIC centre for academic recognition.
atlas-lt.0065: Vilnius University, Vilnius Tech and the Kaunas University of Technology are the schools whose career events and platforms employers use; no programme we read names a target school.
atlas-lt.0066: There is no apprenticeship track for graduates; the equivalent is the curricular internship under a three-party agreement between student, university and company, and an extracurricular volunteer internship for under-29s is capped at two consecutive months and unpaid.
atlas-lt.0067: We could not open the Civil Service or Employment Service pages, so we have no figure for the public sector’s share of graduate hires; the fintech and service-centre numbers (7,800 and 27,000) show where most graduate hiring we could count happens.
atlas-lt.0068: The 2026 quota for non-EU workers (24,706) was used up on 7 September 2026, after which a permit needs a salary of at least €2,893.68 gross a month (€2,411.40 for shortage occupations); 58% of fintechs already employ international staff. The rules are on the Visas page.
atlas-lt.0069: The guides we read disagree on photos and none is official; leave it out unless the advert asks for one.
atlas-lt.0070: The University of Magdeburg’s guide calls the CV a marketing tool for getting an interview: list only relevant education, mention your English and other languages, use a clear layout with brief entries. We found no page that states a page limit; one to two pages is the usual advice.
atlas-lt.0071: The same guide says the cover letter should be short (maximum one page) and typed, and should say why you want this particular position.
atlas-lt.0072: The guide does not put references in the CV; it advises bringing copies of references and diplomas to the interview.
atlas-lt.0073: Bring copies of diplomas and references to the interview; certified translations are needed for degree recognition in a regulated profession, not for ordinary applications.
atlas-lt.0074: Since 27 July 2019 every job advert must state the base salary, as an amount or a range, whether it is gross or net, and the highest pay for the position; breaches can be fined €80 to €880. We found no page on whether application forms ask for your expectation.
atlas-lt.0075: We found no page on background checks in Lithuanian graduate hiring; banks and the public sector can be expected to check more.
atlas-lt.0076: Both work: the Magdeburg guide calls a speculative application to the local office fairly successful and says online applications are becoming more common; the portals and company career pages carry the advertised roles.
atlas-lt.0077: The portals and Swedbank’s steps are online and the fintechs recruit internationally; a non-EU hire from abroad needs a permit first, and the quota is already used up for 2026.
atlas-lt.0078: Many roles in Vilnius do not require Lithuanian, especially at multinationals, and the fintechs and service centres work in English; the bank programmes and Big Four internships we read listed Lithuanian as well, and local firms and the public sector require it.
atlas-lt.0079: Swedbank’s steps are an application on its recruitment portal, calls with a recruiter or interviews with a manager or mentors (possibly with job-related tests or tasks), and then a fixed-term contract; some roles ask for answers in video format.
atlas-lt.0080: The Magdeburg guide says the interview is the most important part of the application in Lithuania: look interested, ask questions, back up achievements with examples, wait to be invited to sit and never criticise former employers.
atlas-lt.0081: We found no page on assessment-centre norms, online tests at the banks and the Big Four, or the time from application to offer.
atlas-lt.0082: Probation is optional and generally cannot exceed three months; one guide allows up to six months for senior management and staff who handle financial or commercial secrets. Either side may end it with three working days’ written notice if the results are unsatisfactory, and a fixed-term contract under six months gets a proportionally shorter probation.
atlas-lt.0083: First contracts for trainees are fixed-term (Swedbank’s Kick Start at €1,200–1,800 gross a month); the advert must state gross or net pay, so check which one the quoted figure is.
atlas-lt.0084: We did not find a page on negotiating, a thirteenth month, notice after probation or the time employers give you to decide, so treat these as unknown rather than as customs.
atlas-lt.0085: A non-EU hire needs a temporary residence permit for work after the employer files a mediation letter (€50) in MIGRIS; the permit costs €160 and takes two to three months, and the worker cannot change employer in the first six months. The 2026 quota of 24,706 was used up on 7 September 2026.
atlas-lt.0086: After the quota is used up, new permits go only to pay of at least €2,893.68 gross a month, or €2,411.40 for occupations on the shortage list; the EU Blue Card needs €3,617.10. A graduate of a Lithuanian university who finds a job within ten years is exempt from the Employment Service’s labour-market opinion.
atlas-lt.0087: Raise it at the first interview: a fintech or centre that already employs international staff (58% of fintechs do) will know the process; EU and EEA citizens need no permit.
atlas-lt.0088: Portals: CVbankas, CV-Online and CV.lt for advertised jobs, the Kaunas University of Technology’s WANTed platform for internships, and company pages such as Swedbank’s Kick Start and Luminor’s programmes.
atlas-lt.0089: Fairs: VU Career Days (March), the Vilnius Tech Career Day, and the career events of other universities; Invest Lithuania lists the fintech and service-centre employers.
atlas-lt.0090: We could not open the national Employment Service site (uzt.lt) and found no graduate-job listing beyond the portals above.
atlas-lt.0091: Assuming English is enough at banks and the Big Four: the Luminor, EY and KPMG postings we read listed Lithuanian as well.
atlas-lt.0092: Missing the spring window: Swedbank hires most actively from February to May and VU Career Days are in March.
atlas-lt.0093: Counting on a state internship scheme: UPinLT’s Vilnius University round ended in August 2024, and Vilnius University’s 2026 internship scholarship for final-year master’s students had closed its applications by October 2026.
atlas-lt.0094: Assuming a permit is still available: the 2026 quota for non-EU workers ran out on 7 September 2026.
atlas-lt.0095: Writing a long cover letter: the Magdeburg guide says one typed page at most.
atlas-lt.0096: Banks ask for both: a Luminor graduate programme in corporate banking in Vilnius (a 2023 posting) required fluent English and Lithuanian; the fintechs hire in English.
atlas-lt.0097: EY’s audit internship listed English and Lithuanian, and KPMG’s ERP internship asked for fluent Lithuanian and effective English; no certificate level is stated on the pages.
atlas-lt.0098: The fintechs and service centres hire in English, and a Vilnius University guide says many roles in Vilnius are open to non-Lithuanian speakers; Shift4 runs its largest European tech centre in Vilnius.
atlas-lt.0099: Nord Security’s products and customers are international; we found no page stating its hiring language or a level.
atlas-lt.0100: Local firms and the public sector require Lithuanian; we could not open the Civil Service pages to read the level.
atlas-lt.0101: In 2025, 92.7% of Lithuanian tertiary graduates aged 20–34 who finished within the last three years were in work (EU 85.3%), and unemployment among 15-to-24-year-olds was 14.1% (EU 15.2%).
atlas-lt.0102: No national figure for how many interns or trainees are kept; 77% of fintechs plan to expand their teams in 2026, which is the best signal we found of demand for new graduates.
atlas-lt.0103: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no visa or work permit. Staying more than three months, apply through MIGRIS for the EU residence certificate: €10, issued within a month, valid up to five years.
atlas-lt.0104: The university files the invitation in MIGRIS free of charge; you then apply for the permit, which already includes the right to work.
atlas-lt.0105: Since 22 May 2026, bachelor’s students in years 1 and 2 may work 20 hours a week in term; from year 3, and on master’s and PhD courses, up to 40.
atlas-lt.0106: A non-EU student with a permit from another EU country in an EU programme can study here up to 360 days on a free university notification.
atlas-lt.0107: €576.50 a month plus €1,153 for the return: €8,071 for a year
atlas-lt.0108: €80, or €320 for a decision in a month
